activities.anchor: Two numbers describe most of an asset's character
activities.caption: fill the character sheet — level, width, drag
activities.name: dvCharacterCloze

config.text: An asset returning about 7 per cent a year with 20 per cent volatility will, in a typical year, land anywhere between %%0%% and +27 — and the return you actually compound is roughly the arithmetic mean minus half the %%1%%. A 20 per cent volatile asset compounds about %%2%% percentage points below its average.
config.hint: The typical-year band, the variance term, and the drag in points.

activities.anchor: measures how much excess return each unit of risk buys
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the fund comparison
activities.name: dvSharpeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this fund-comparison note is wrong — click it:
lines: The Sharpe ratio is excess return divided by volatility.
A fund earning 9 per cent with 18 per cent volatility scores about 0.39.
The fund with the higher headline return is the better engine.
The 7-per-cent fund with 10 per cent volatility scores 0.50 and wins.
Diversification raises the ratio by stripping out risk that carries no extra return.
config.correction: The question is never 'which return is higher?' but which is higher per unit of risk — the 0.50 engine beats the 0.39 despite the lower headline number.
config.why: Return and risk always travel together, so professionals quote them as a ratio — and the rational comparison is per unit of risk, never the raw headline.

activities.anchor: The general law for many uncorrelated assets
activities.caption: file the portfolios by whether the √n law fires
activities.name: dvSqrtBuckets

config.prompt: The √n rule — file each portfolio by whether the law can fire:

items.label: one hundred independent stocks, each 30 per cent volatile
equities, bonds, geographies, currencies — different drivers
thirty technology stocks sharing one macro driver
ten more names from the same sector

config.why: Diversify across kinds, not within one kind — the law only fires when the drivers don't coincide; thirty tech names share rates and tech spending.

activities.caption: drag the divider — owning a lot vs owning drivers
activities.name: dvDriversCompare

config.prompt: Two portfolios, one feeling — drag the divider:

before.label: Owns a lot
before.text: Thirty technology stocks — feels diversified, behaves like one large bet: one macro driver, correlations clustered near 1.

after.label: Owns drivers
after.text: Twelve assets across stocks, bonds, countries and styles — genuinely spread, because the drivers don't coincide.

config.why: The 12-asset portfolio is smaller on paper and larger in substance — correlation, not count, is the dial.

activities.anchor: the curve of risk reduction is steep at first and then flattens
activities.caption: call the number — names enough
activities.name: dvNamesEstimate

config.prompt: For a US stock portfolio, roughly how many individual names eliminate about 90 per cent of diversifiable risk?
config.why: The classic finding is 30–40 names: going from 1 to 10 removes a large share, 20–30 captures most of the rest, and beyond roughly 40 you are adding little but fees and tracking burden.

activities.caption: pin the glide path's starting altitude
activities.name: dvGlidePlace

config.prompt: A target-date fund twenty-five years from retirement starts its glide path at roughly what equity share?
config.why: Roughly 90 per cent equities, stepping down toward 50–60 as the date approaches — risk capacity declines as the spending date nears, because sequence risk dominates short spans.

config.root: October 2008. Nearly everything falls together — equities, credit, commodities, hedge strategies.

start.text: Your 100 stocks held through it. What happened to the √n protection?

choices.label: It held — a hundred names guarantees safety
choices.feedback: It assumed independence that no longer existed: the law never fired when the shock arrived.

choices.label: It never fired — correlations converged toward 1
choices.feedback: Exactly: the removal of everyday risk was real, but tail risk was never covered.

choices.label: The 60/40 bond hedge saved the year
choices.feedback: Not in 2008 — and 2022 broke it from the other side, when inflation pushed rates up and stocks and bonds fell together.

end.text: The mitigations: assets with structurally different crisis behaviour — cash and short government bonds are the reliable ones — and the emergency buffer kept outside markets entirely.

config.why: A portfolio that fell 30 per cent instead of 50 was still doing its job — the mistake is expecting the square-root law to survive an event that breaks independence.
